desc:
Each row of points is a point [x, y] in the plane, and no point is the origin (0, 0). The angle of a point is the counterclockwise angle from the positive x-axis to the ray from the origin through the point, in the half-open range [0, 360) degrees. So (1, 0) has angle 0, (0, 1) has 90, (-1, 0) has 180 and (0, -1) has 270.

Return the points sorted by angle in ascending order. Points on the same ray from the origin are ordered by distance from the origin, closer first. Equal points may appear several times.

Example: [[1, 1], [-1, 0], [2, 0], [0, -3], [2, 2], [0, 5]] gives [[2, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [0, 5], [-1, 0], [0, -3]].
constraints: Each point has exactly 2 coordinates, -10,000 ≤ x, y ≤ 10,000
hints: Sorting by atan2 is tempting, but floating point can misorder or tie directions that are very close or exactly equal. Can you compare two directions with integers only?

The cross product ax * by - ay * bx is positive when b is counterclockwise from a (within a half turn). It only works for angles less than 180 degrees apart, so split the plane into two half-planes first.
Half 0 holds points with y > 0 or (y == 0 and x > 0), half 1 holds the rest. Sort by half, then by the cross product within a half, then by squared distance.
editorial: Avoid floating point: two points have exactly the same direction when their cross product is zero (and they lie on the same side), and atan2 may not report that faithfully. Use exact integer arithmetic. Coordinates are at most 104, so cross products stay below 2 * 108.

The cross product tells which of two vectors is counterclockwise of the other only when the angle between them is less than 180 degrees. Therefore classify each point into the half-plane [0, 180) (y > 0, or y == 0 and x > 0) or [180, 360). Order by half first. Inside one half any two points are less than 180 degrees apart, so a comparator returning negative when cross(a, b) > 0 is a valid total preorder. For zero cross product (same ray) the closer point, measured by x*x + y*y, goes first.
Sorting with this comparator takes O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
